newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian businesses call for lower tax burden.
newsitem.headline: Serbian businesses call for lower tax burden.

text.p: A group of Serbian businessmen said on Wednesday proposed tax changes could threaten the country's entire economic activity and frighten off scarce foreign investment.
The government has proposed to launch a tax on commercial lending rates and to tax equipment imported by foreign firms.
The proposal also assumes an increase in the minimum sales tax to 10 from 7 percent and the launch of a 10 percent sales tax for agricultural machinery and manufacturing equipment.
The Economic Department of the Serbian Chamber of Commerce warned taxing commercial bank credits and lending rates as a way to control interest rates will prove futile.

"Interest rates are already enormous and our economy cannot endure the burden of higher interest rates," Djordje Djukic, president of the department and a member of the central bank Board of Governors, said.
Djukic said any taxation would translate into higher commercial lending rates. Average lending rates now stand at around 15 percent per month.
Economists feared the government would try to limit interest rate rises by exercising administrative control over the banks -- a policy Djukic insisted would prove damaging.

"I remind you of April 1993 when the government introduced administrative control on lending rates and rates on deposits. Such control was a part of the populist policy that lead to hyperinflation," he said.
Economy Department secretary Branislava Zunjic said the proposed sales tax hike would harm the economy.
"The seven percent sales tax on staples is high enough and if raised it will affect prices," Zunjic told Reuters, adding it could harm the dinar exchange rate.
The department also warned taxing equipment imported by foreigners could discourage the few who were willing to invest.

"Foreigners are very practical. They want to know if their deposit is subject to tax? What is the level of the tax? Can they sell their earned dinars on the local forex market and repatriate profits? They don't care about the local tax maze," Djukic said.
"We demand better tax treatement of foreigners. We want the state to abolish those (equipment) taxes and to show it wants to create a more convenient investment climate," he said.
